title: What is Long? What is Round?
short: What is Long? What is Round?
intro: In Class 1 Maths Chapter 2, What is Long? What is Round?, the topics are: Long and Round Things, objects of the same shape, rolling and sliding, building with shapes. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Long and Round Things
Things around us have shapes
Objects of the Same Shape
Things that look different (colour, size, use) can have the SAME shape
Rolling and Sliding
A thing that can turn over and over on the side touching the floor (a full round side, like a wheel) ROLLS; a thing that cannot ...
Building with Shapes
Shapes help us build

items: Things around us have shapes. Some are long (they stretch far one way, like a pencil box or our legs) and some are round (curved all round, like a ball or our face). Some things can be seen both ways.
Look around — shapes are everywhere, even on our body
Long = stretches far one way; round = curved all round, no corners
Some things are both — say why
Things that look different (colour, size, use) can have the SAME shape. A football and a beach ball are both ball-shaped; a birthday cap and a paper cone are both cap-shaped.
Same shape ≠ same colour or size
Families: ball, cap, glass, box (and dome)
Look at the whole object: a point? corners? round all over? flat round ends? round top and flat bottom?

A thing that can turn over and over on the side touching the floor (a full round side, like a wheel) ROLLS; a thing that cannot turn over SLIDES (moves without turning). Things with a full round side and a flat side can do both.
Can turn over and over on the side touching the floor (full round side) → rolls
Flat side on the floor → slides
Full round side + flat side → can do both
Curved but cannot turn over (spoon, bun, idli) → rocks and slides, does not roll

Shapes help us build. Flat-faced shapes stay on top of each other and make tall, steady towers (the wider the bottom, the steadier); round shapes roll off. We can make houses, toys, robots, puppets and clay models from shapes around us.
Flat bottom + flat top → good for a tower
The wider the bottom, the steadier the tower
Round all over → rolls off
Pointed top → only at the very top
Wrong: A thing can only be long OR round — one answer is right, the other is wrong. Right: A tumbler or bottle is long (tall) and also round (its mouth) — both answers are right if you say why
Wrong: Things of the same colour have the same shape (red ball and red box). Right: Colour does not decide shape — look at corners, points and curves
Wrong: Every round thing always rolls. Right: A striker is a flat disc with a round edge (a coin shape): lying on its flat face it slides; it can roll only on its round edge
Wrong: Any shape can go anywhere in a tower. Right: A ball rolls off and a cap's point holds nothing — flat-topped shapes go below, pointed ones on the very top

sol_items: B. Match the objects which are similar in shape: Drum - candle; football - beach ball; carton - gift box; bun - idli; birthday cap - paper cone.
Why did the dholak roll so fast?: It is round and the path was a slope.
Carrom: It slides on its flat face.
Why did one striker roll instead of sliding?: It was on its round edge, so it rolled.
C. Do you see things which can both roll and slide: Yes. Bottle, glass, tin can.
B. Make towers: Flat shapes like boxes and books. Balls roll off.
imp_items: Is a plate long or round? Is a rope long or round?
plate - round; rope - long
Match the gift box with a thing of the same shape: a ball, a carton or a paper cone
carton
Tick the shape similar to a glass: a tin can, a football or a funnel
tin can
A tin can lies on its side and then stands up. Does it roll, slide or both?
both - it rolls lying down and slides standing up
Which goes at the very top of a tower: a matchbox, a paper cone or a book?
paper cone

title: Mango Treat
intro: In Class 1 Maths Chapter 3, Mango Treat, the topics are: One More: Numbers 1 to 9, counting objects 1 to 9, showing numbers with numerals, fingers and dots, more, less or same, numbers in order 1 to 9. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: One More: Numbers 1 to 9
When one more joins a group, the number becomes the next counting number: 1, 2, 3 … 9
Counting Objects 1 to 9
Touch and count each thing once; the last number we say tells how many
Showing Numbers with Numerals, Fingers and Dots
The same number can be written as a numeral and a name, and shown with fingers or dots in many different ways — it stays the same ...
More, Less or Same
Match the things of two groups one to one: if one group has things left over it has more; if none are left over they are the same
Numbers in Order 1 to 9
Numbers 1 to 9 come in a fixed order; each number is 1 more than the one before, so a number that comes later is bigger

items: When one more joins a group, the number becomes the next counting number: 1, 2, 3 … 9.
1 more than 1 is 2, 1 more than 2 is 3 … 1 more than 8 is 9
At the end 9 ate the mango: 1 squirrel and 8 birds
Touch and count each thing once; the last number we say tells how many. To make a group of a number, stop when you reach it; two groups can be counted together as one.
Touch each thing once, say one number for each
The last number said tells how many
Count out: stop when you reach the number asked
Two groups together: count all the things of both groups

notes.h: Showing Numbers with Numerals, Fingers and Dots
items: The same number can be written as a numeral and a name, and shown with fingers or dots in many different ways — it stays the same number.
One full hand shows 5
6 to 9 need both hands: 5 and some more
Each number has a numeral and a name: 7 Seven
Any fingers, any dot pattern — the count decides the number
Match the things of two groups one to one: if one group has things left over it has more; if none are left over they are the same.
Match one to one
Left over → more; none left → same
Less → share
Numbers 1 to 9 come in a fixed order; each number is 1 more than the one before, so a number that comes later is bigger.
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 — fixed order
Just after = 1 more; just before = 1 less
Comes later when counting → bigger; 9 is the biggest of 1 to 9
Wrong: Only birds are counted — so 8 ate the mango. Right: The squirrel ate too: 1 squirrel and 8 birds make 9
Wrong: Counting a thing twice, or skipping one, in a picture. Right: Tick or dot each thing as you count it, so each is counted once — in a crowd, count heads
Wrong: 3 shown with different fingers is a different number. Right: Any 3 fingers show 3 — only the count matters
Wrong: The group with bigger things (bananas, a tall stack) is always 'more'. Right: More is about how many, not how big — match or count
Wrong: A numeral drawn bigger on the page is a bigger number. Right: Size of the drawing does not matter — 9 is bigger than 3 however it is drawn

sol_items: D. What is 1 more than 1, 1 more than 2 ... up to : 1 more than 1 is 2; than 2 is 3; than 3 is 4; than 4 is 5; than 5 is 6; than 6 is 7; than 7 is 8; than 8 is 9.
Match the number of birds with the number of finge: 4 birds - 4 fingers; 5 birds - 3 + 2 fingers; 7 birds - 5 + 2 fingers; 9 birds - 5 + 4 fingers.
Match the fingers with the correct number of dots: 3 + 2 fingers - 5 dots; 3 fingers - 3 dots; 4 fingers - 4 dots; 4 + 2 fingers - 6 dots.
How did you find more, less or equal? Why share? What i...: Match one to one. We share so everyone gets a turn. Ekta Diwas, 31st October, is a day of togetherness.
A. Tick the one which is more in number: Bananas are more.
B. Tick the one which is less: The plate of 5 is less.
imp_items: What is 1 more than 6?
Count the stars: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★
Colour 6 of these 9 circles: ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○
Colour exactly 6 circles, stop at 6; 3 stay white
Groups of 3, 4 and 6 balls: which two together have 9?
3 and 6 (3 and 4 make 7, 4 and 6 make 10)
There are 3 birds. How many fingers match them?
3 fingers
Show 3 fingers in two different ways. Is it still 3?
Yes, any 3 fingers show 3

title: Making 10
intro: In Class 1 Maths Chapter 4, Making 10, the topics are: Seeing Numbers in Dot Patterns, zero, 9 and 1 more makes 10, number pairs of 5, number pairs of 10, counting up to 20, comparing and ordering numbers up to 20. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Seeing Numbers in Dot Patterns
Small numbers (1 to 9) can be known at a glance from the shape their dots make, without counting one by one
Zero
When nothing is left, the number is zero, written 0
9 and 1 More Makes 10
9 and 1 more makes 10
Number Pairs of 5
5 can be split into two parts in different ways: 1 and 4, 2 and 3, 3 and 2, 4 and 1, 5 and 0
Number Pairs of 10
10 can be split into two parts: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5 (and the same pairs turned round)
Counting up to 20
Numbers 11 to 20 are one ten and some more: 10 and 1 is 11, 10 and 4 is 14, 10 and 10 is 20
Comparing and Ordering Numbers up to 20
Each number is one more than the number before it, so a number that comes later when counting is bigger

items: Small numbers (1 to 9) can be known at a glance from the shape their dots make, without counting one by one.
Dice shapes: 4 = square, 5 = square with one in the middle, 6 = two rows of 3
Count once to check what you saw
When nothing is left, the number is zero, written 0. Zero is a number like one and two.
None left = 0
Zero comes just before 1 when counting
9 and 1 more makes 10. Ten is all the fingers of two hands, a full string of 10 beads, a full ten frame.
9 and 1 more = 10
Ten frame: 2 rows of 5
5 can be split into two parts in different ways: 1 and 4, 2 and 3, 3 and 2, 4 and 1, 5 and 0.
Fingers up and fingers folded on one hand always make 5
10 can be split into two parts: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5 (and the same pairs turned round).
Numbers 11 to 20 are one ten and some more: 10 and 1 is 11, 10 and 4 is 14, 10 and 10 is 20.
11 to 20 are 10 and some more: 15 is 10 and 5 (p.41)
(added) In 15, the 1 stands for the full ten and the 5 for the extra ones

notes.h: Comparing and Ordering Numbers up to 20
items: Each number is one more than the number before it, so a number that comes later when counting is bigger.
Later in counting = bigger
15 is bigger than 11 because it is 4 more (p.46)
(added) For two numbers from 11 to 19, the one with more extra ones is bigger
Wrong: Dots spread far apart are MORE than the same dots kept close. Right: The number stays the same whatever the arrangement — 4 in a line and 4 in a square are both 4
Wrong: Zero is not a number — it is just 'nothing'. Right: Zero is a number: it tells HOW MANY when there are none
Wrong: 10 is written with one new sign, like 9. Right: 10 is written with a 1 (one full ten) and a 0 (added)
Wrong: 5 and 0 is not a pair because 0 is nothing. Right: 5 and 0 makes 5 — when the stick is after all 5 seeds, the other side has 0
Wrong: The partner of 1 for 10 is 4 (as in pairs of 5). Right: For 10 the partner of 1 is 9 — use two hands, not one
Wrong: Fourteen is written 41 because we say 'four' first. Right: Fourteen is 10 and 4, so the 1 (the ten) is written first: 14

sol_items: How many buttons are left each time? How many at t: Four, three, two, one, zero buttons. At the end 0 buttons are left.
Write the number of birds sitting on the branch: 3, 2, 1, 0 (no bird is on the branch).
A. Count and draw beads to make a string of 10 bea: Draw 4 more for 6, 3 more for 7, 6 more for 4, 8 more for 2.
B. Draw buttons to make a ten frame of buttons: Draw 7 more for 3, 4 more for 6, 8 more for 2, 9 more for 1.
Write the number pairs of 5 separated by the stick: 1 and 4; 2 and 3; 3 and 2; 4 and 1; 5 and 0.
Let us Play: your friend shows 3 fingers. Show fingers ...: Show 2 fingers. 3 and 2 make 5.
imp_items: A card shows dots like the six on a dice: 3 dots in the top row and 3 in the bottom row. How many dots?
Ravi has 3 balloons and one bursts every minute. How many are left after 2 bursts? After 3 bursts?
1; then 0
How many fish are in an empty bucket?
0 (none)
Write the number 0 two times. Where do you start?
Start at the top, go round and close the loop: 0 0
Count the crayons: 7 crayons lie in a row. Touch each once. How many?
A string has 7 beads. How many more beads make 10?

title: How Many?
intro: In Class 1 Maths Chapter 5, How Many?, the topics are: Adding Two Groups: Altogether, adding with fingers, dice and beads, adding on a number strip, number pairs that make a number, addition stories, taking away: how many are left?, how many dots are hidden?, subtracting on a number strip. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Adding Two Groups: Altogether
When groups are put together we count them all to know how many altogether
Adding with Fingers, Dice and Beads
Fingers, dice dots and beads show each number as objects; counting all of them gives the sum
Adding on a Number Strip
On a number strip, start at the first number and hop forward as many steps as the second number; where you land is the sum
Number Pairs That Make a Number
Many different pairs of numbers make the same total: 7 + 1, 6 + 2, 5 + 3, 4 + 4 all make 8
Addition Stories
In a story sum, find the two numbers; the words altogether, in total and in all tell us to add
Taking Away: How Many Are Left?
When some go away, we take them away and count the ones that are left
How Many Dots Are Hidden?
On a ten dots card, hidden dots and visible dots together make 10, so hidden = 10 − visible
Subtracting on a Number Strip
To take away on a number strip, stand on the first number and hop backwards as many steps as the second number; where you land is ...

items: When groups are put together we count them all to know how many altogether. We write it with + (and) and = (altogether make): 4 + 2 = 6.
Altogether / in all / total → put together → add
+ is read 'and', = is read 'altogether make'
Adding makes the group bigger

notes.h: Adding with Fingers, Dice and Beads
items: Fingers, dice dots and beads show each number as objects; counting all of them gives the sum.
Show each number as objects, then count all
Adding 0 keeps the number the same
To find who scores more, add first, then compare
On a number strip, start at the first number and hop forward as many steps as the second number; where you land is the sum.
Stand on the first number, hop the second number forward
First hop lands on the next number
Standing or lying, the sum is the same

notes.h: Number Pairs That Make a Number
items: Many different pairs of numbers make the same total: 7 + 1, 6 + 2, 5 + 3, 4 + 4 all make 8. Turning a pair around (1 + 7) gives the same total.
One number, many pairs
First up one, second down one — total stays
Turn-around pairs have the same total
In a story sum, find the two numbers; the words altogether, in total and in all tell us to add.
Find the two numbers
Find the clue word
Answer with the thing counted

notes.h: Taking Away: How Many Are Left?
items: When some go away, we take them away and count the ones that are left. We write it with − (take away): 6 − 2 = 4.
Left, flew away, ate, took away → take away
Start − gone = left
The number left is smaller than the start
On a ten dots card, hidden dots and visible dots together make 10, so hidden = 10 − visible.
Hidden + visible = total
More hidden → fewer visible
Pairs of 10 tell the hidden dots at once
To take away on a number strip, stand on the first number and hop backwards as many steps as the second number; where you land is what is left.
Stand on the first number, hop back the second
Hop: the first hop lands on the number just before · Colour: colour the start too, the answer is the next square
Check: add back what you took away
Wrong: 4 + 2 means write 4 and 2 side by side (42). Right: + means put the groups together and count all: 4 + 2 = 6
Wrong: 4 + 0 is 0 (or 40). Right: 0 means no fingers on the second hand, so 4 + 0 = 4
Wrong: Count the number you stand on as the first hop (5 + 3: 5, 6, 7 → 7). Right: the first hop lands on the NEXT number: 6, 7, 8 → 8
Wrong: 1 + 7 makes a different number from 7 + 1. Right: turning the pair around gives the same total, 8
Wrong: We add only when the story says 'add'. Right: altogether, in total and in all also mean add
Wrong: Taking away makes more. Right: after taking away, fewer are left

sol_items: Park picture: how many children are playing, how many j...: Count the children playing and those who join; put both groups together.
Tell how many altogether: 4 children and 2 children; 3 ...: 4 + 2 = 6; 3 + 1 = 4; 3 + 2 = 5; 4 + 3 = 7.
Count the fingers: 7, 5, 8, 4, 8
Kishore and Nitya dice totals A to E: how many times di...: A 6 vs 5, B 4 vs 7, C 5 vs 8, D 4 vs 5, E 6 vs 7. Kishore won 1 time (A). Nitya won 4 times.
Beads and String: 7, 6, 9, 9, 10
imp_items: 5 apples and 3 apples altogether make how many apples?
8 apples
A tower has 5 blocks and 2 more blocks are put on top. How many blocks now?
7 blocks
Kishore rolls 2 and 6, Nitya rolls 3 and 4. Who scores more?
Kishore: 2 + 6 = 8 is more than 3 + 4 = 7
Hop 3 + 5 on the number strip. Where do you land?
Standing sum: 7 on top, + 2 below. What goes under the line?
Write two pairs that make 7.

intro: In Class 1 Maths Chapter 6, Vegetable Farm, the topics are: Adding Two Groups, counting on to add, split into ten and ones, addition stories, subtraction, same answer, different ways, problem stories. topics: Adding Two Groups
When two groups are put together, we count all the things to find how many there are altogether, and write it as 7 + 5 = 12
Counting On to Add
To add, start at the first number and count on the second number one bead or one hop at a time; the number where you stop is the ...
Split into Ten and Ones
A teen number is a ten and some ones (12 = 10 + 2)
Addition Stories
In a story, words like 'in all', 'altogether', 'got … more' and 'now' tell us groups are put together, so we add the two numbers ...
Subtraction
Subtraction means taking away: cross out the things taken away and count what is left (15 − 9 = 6)
Same Answer, Different Ways
An addition and a subtraction can give the same number: Anjali jumps 2 ahead from 6 and Renu jumps 7 back from 15 — both reach 8
Problem Stories
In a problem story, the words tell us whether things are put together (add) or taken away (subtract); some stories need two ...

items: When two groups are put together, we count all the things to find how many there are altogether, and write it as 7 + 5 = 12.
Putting together makes more: the total is bigger than each group (unless one group is empty).
To add, start at the first number and count on the second number one bead or one hop at a time; the number where you stop is the sum.
Count on from the bigger number.
Many pairs make the same sum: 5 + 3 = 8 and 6 + 2 = 8.
A teen number is a ten and some ones (12 = 10 + 2). Add the ones first, then join them to the ten: 12 + 6 = 10 + 2 + 6 = 10 + 8 = 18.
In a story, words like 'in all', 'altogether', 'got … more' and 'now' tell us groups are put together, so we add the two numbers in our own way.
Find the two numbers → find the asking words → add in your own way (count on or split into ten and ones).
Subtraction means taking away: cross out the things taken away and count what is left (15 − 9 = 6). On a number strip we jump back.
An addition and a subtraction can give the same number: Anjali jumps 2 ahead from 6 and Renu jumps 7 back from 15 — both reach 8.
Jump ahead = add; jump back = subtract.
Make your own pairs: 10 + 4 and 16 − 2 both make 14.
In a problem story, the words tell us whether things are put together (add) or taken away (subtract); some stories need two steps, some ask how many more, some ask how many were given away.
Check the answer: put the parts back together (8 + 6 = 14).
Wrong: For the second basket, start again from 1 and write that number as the answer (9 + 4 = 4). Right: Keep counting on from where the first basket ended: 10, 11, 12, 13 → 13
Wrong: For 13 + 4, count 13, 14, 15, 16 and say 16 (counting the start number again). Right: Start AT 13 and say the NEXT numbers: 14, 15, 16, 17 → 17
Wrong: 10 + 8 is written 108. Right: 10 + 8 is one ten and 8 ones = 18
Wrong: Sheena 'got 6 more' — so the answer is 6. Right: 6 is only what she got; she now has 12 + 6 = 18
Wrong: Count the crossed-out things and write that as the answer (16 − 4 = 4). Right: Count the things NOT crossed out — those are left: 12
Wrong: Adding always gives a bigger answer than subtracting, so they can never be equal. Right: 6 + 2 = 8 and 15 − 7 = 8 — an addition and a subtraction can give the same number

sol_items: Show 13 + 4, 14 + 5, 6 + 8 and 5 + 7 on the ginlad: 17, 19, 14 and 12.
Hop and find the sum: 16, 18 and 16.
Gauri did 12 + 6 as 10 + 2 + 6 = 10 + 8. Can you do it ...: 18 (counting on gives the same answer)
imp_items: 6 brinjals and 3 brinjals: how many altogether?
13 + 5 on the bead string
3 + 15 = ? (start from the bigger number)
Find two numbers that make 17 (one pair)
Rani has 9 marbles and gets 5 more. How many now?
14 + 5 the ten-and-ones way

title: Lina's Family
intro: In Class 1 Maths Chapter 7, Lina's Family, the topics are: Tall and Short, long and short, thick and thin, near and far, measuring with handspan, fingers and footspan, heavier and lighter, holds more, holds less, using the right amount of water. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Tall and Short
To compare heights, stand people or things side by side on the same floor and look at the tops
Long and Short, Thick and Thin
For things lying down we say long / short; for how fat or wide a thing is we say thick / thin
Near and Far
Near means a short way to go; far means a long way
Measuring with Handspan, Fingers and Footspan
We can measure length with our body: count handspans for a table, fingers for small things like a key, footspans for the floor of ...
Heavier and Lighter
Lift two things, one in each hand: the one that pulls your hand down more is heavier, the other is lighter
Holds More, Holds Less
To find which container holds more water, fill both with the SAME cup and count
Using the Right Amount of Water
Water is very useful, so we take only as much as a job needs: a mug to brush teeth, a bucket to bathe, a jug for two glasses of ...

items: To compare heights, stand people or things side by side on the same floor and look at the tops. Two things: taller / shorter. Many things: tallest / shortest.
Feet on the same floor, then look at the heads
-er for two (taller), -est for many (tallest)
Taller than one person can still be shorter than another

notes.h: Long and Short, Thick and Thin
items: For things lying down we say long / short; for how fat or wide a thing is we say thick / thin. Line up one end to compare length.
Line up one end, look at the other end
Long/short = length; thick/thin = how fat
Near means a short way to go; far means a long way. Near and far are always FROM some place: nearest is the one we reach first.
Say near/far FROM a place
Nearest = reached first, farthest = reached last

notes.h: Measuring with Handspan, Fingers and Footspan
items: We can measure length with our body: count handspans for a table, fingers for small things like a key, footspans for the floor of a room. Guess first, then measure.
Guess first, then measure
Handspan for a table, fingers for a key, footspan for a room
No gaps, no overlaps
Lift two things, one in each hand: the one that pulls your hand down more is heavier, the other is lighter. A full thing is heavier than the same thing empty.
Lift one in each hand
Full is heavier than empty
Big does not always mean heavy
To find which container holds more water, fill both with the SAME cup and count. More cups to fill it = it holds more.
Same cup for both
More cups = holds more
Bigger pourer = fewer pours

notes.h: Using the Right Amount of Water
items: Water is very useful, so we take only as much as a job needs: a mug to brush teeth, a bucket to bathe, a jug for two glasses of lemon water, a mug for a plant.
Smallest container that is enough
Never waste water
Wrong: Lina is the tallest because she is standing on a stool. Right: The stool lifts her; compare everyone standing on the same floor

topics: What Is a Pattern?

Repeating Patterns of Three Parts

items: A pattern follows a rule we can say: a part that comes again and again in the same order (toran: leaf, flower, leaf, flower), or the same change each time (1, 2, 3 triangles — met later). Festival decorations, nature, clothes and buildings are full of patterns.

In a growing pattern each step has one more than the step before; in a shrinking pattern each step has one less.
Growing: one more each time.
Shrinking: one less each time.
Count each step and write the number under it.
In a number pattern the numbers go up (or down) by the same jump each time. Find the jump, then fill the missing numbers.
Find the jump between two numbers next to each other.
Add the jump to go forward; take it away when the numbers go down.

We can make our own patterns with finger prints, vegetable prints, kolam, objects, pictures and even actions like clapping.
Choose a repeating part, then repeat it in the same order.
